uncited: Physics-Based Image Formation Models define the differentiable forward operator $\mathcal{P}$ that maps a 3D (or 4D) volume representation to 2D projection images, serving as the core component in inverse rendering pipelines.

Unlike generic differentiable renderers, these models are tailored to specific physical acquisition modalities (e.g., X-ray absorption, ultrasound wave propagation) to ensure physical consistency and computational efficiency.

They distinguish themselves from siblings like [Neural Adaptive Tomography](1862-neural-adaptive-tomography-neat.md) by explicitly modeling the underlying physics (such as linear absorption or coupled wave equations) rather than relying solely on learned neural priors or adaptive sampling strategies.
All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward projection operator $\mathcal{P}$ and its adjoint (back-projection) $\mathcal{P}^T$.

The term $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}}$ is the residual gradient in projection space (e.g., $p - \hat{p}$ for MSE), and $\mathcal{P}^T$ is the back-projection operator [S2][S3, unofficial].
**Backward Projection (Adjoint):** Distributing the error from the 2D detector plane back into the 3D volume.
This is mathematically the transpose of the forward operator, ensuring stable convergence in iterative methods [S2][S3, unofficial].
Double the resolution in each dimension after 10 iterations.
The family originates from the application of differentiable rendering techniques to tomographic reconstruction.

The field has since expanded to include specialized physics-based models for modalities like ultrasound, where simple ray-tracing is insufficient to capture wave phenomena [5511-b-mode-image-reconstruction.md].
